title: Postcards and Interior
premise: After his mother's funeral, Wren Brightwater returns to the crumbling family house to sort her estate, feeling like a caretaker of a life he never understood. Behind her wardrobe he finds forty years of undelivered letters addressed to a man named Elias Okonkwo — letters she wrote and never sent, and one from Elias that arrived and was hidden. Following their thread, Wren discovers his mother helped cover up an old injustice that cost Elias his home and livelihood, and that the house itself sits on land never rightfully theirs. As the council's demolition date approaches, Wren must choose between preserving his inheritance and returning what was stolen; in the end, he signs the house over to Elias's daughter, walks away with only the letters, and finally feels he belongs somewhere — to the truth.
about_author: Ulyana Halloran is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging unclaimed estates in coastal towns, where she first encountered boxes of letters no one had ever opened. She writes literary fiction about the objects families leave behind and the debts they carry forward.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Wren, third-person limited, moves through his late mother's house after the funeral, sleeping in a guest room and eating off paper plates because nothing feels like his. Neighbors offer condolences he can't answer. The emotional beat is estrangement: grief experienced as displacement, a son inventorying a stranger's life.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing the bedroom for an estate sale, Wren pries loose a panel behind the wardrobe and finds a shoebox: decades of unsent letters to Elias Okonkwo, plus one opened letter with a 1987 postmark. POV stays with Wren. The beat is vertigo — the discovery that his mother's silence had an address.

chapters.title: What She Never Sent
chapters.summary: Wren reads the letters chronologically through the night, learning of a deep friendship that curdled after something unnamed in 1986. His mother's voice on the page is funnier and more alive than the woman he knew. Beat: intimacy with the dead, and the first flicker of anger at what was concealed.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photograph
chapters.summary: A photograph shows his mother and a young Black man laughing outside the very house. Wren tracks down Mrs. Adeyemi, an elderly neighbor, who goes quiet when she sees the name Okonkwo. Her partial answers deepen the mystery. Beat: the past pushing back against polite forgetting.

chapters.title: Elias
chapters.summary: Through Mrs. Adeyemi and county records, Wren learns Elias lost his boatyard and home after a fire and a fraudulent insurance claim — one his mother witnessed and stayed silent about, likely at his grandfather's insistence. Beat: moral nausea as inheritance reveals itself as theft.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The council posts notice: the house and three others are condemned for redevelopment in six weeks. Wren realizes the truth will be buried with the building itself. He finds a lead — Elias may have a daughter, Naomi, living two towns over. Beat: urgency colliding with dread.

chapters.title: Naomi
chapters.summary: Wren visits Naomi Okonkwo, a carpenter rebuilding boats by hand, and confesses clumsily. She is neither forgiving nor cruel; she asks him to prove what he claims before she'll hear more. Beat: humiliation as the beginning of honesty — he cannot inherit absolution.

chapters.title: Paper Trails
chapters.summary: Rising action: Wren digs into deeds, insurance files, and his grandfather's papers, assembling evidence of the fraud while the demolition clock runs down. His brother arrives demanding he stop shaming the family name. Beat: justice outside the law taking shape — the statute expired long ago; only restitution remains possible.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Climax: among the final unsent letters, dated weeks before her death, Wren finds his mother's confession and apology, finished but never mailed. He reads it aloud to Naomi in the emptying house. His brother threatens legal action; Wren signs the property over anyway. Beat: forgiveness offered, not guaranteed.

chapters.title: Forwarding Address
chapters.summary: Resolution: on demolition day, Wren watches the excavators arrive, holding only the box of letters, which Naomi has asked him to keep until she's ready. He mails the last letter to her, properly stamped. Walking through town, he feels, for the first time, like an owner of his own life. Beat: belonging earned through letting go.
